summary: Proposes a way to carry SMTP mail transfer over the virtual circuits provided by the X.25 network standard from CCITT.

eli5.summary: Email normally rides on one kind of road. This shows how to send it on a different kind of road, an X.25 phone-like connection, instead.

questions: sending internet mail over x.25 networks
how does smtp work over x25
subtitle: Running SMTP mail transfer directly over X.25 virtual circuits instead of TCP.

tldr.problem: RFC 821 suggested running a reliable protocol such as TCP on top of X.25, but X.25 networks had become reliable enough to carry SMTP directly.
tldr.mechanism: One X.25 virtual circuit is opened per SMTP session, with a fixed protocol ID in the call user data, and the SMTP text flows over it with its own timeouts and closing rules.
tldr.outcome: The author reports the procedures worked in production across 24 PSDNs in 22 countries.

today: RFC 1090 proposes a standard for SMTP on X.25. The unit metadata lists its status as unknown and shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The SMTP it builds on is defined in RFC 821.

sections.title: SMTP Straight onto X.25
sections.content:
RFC 821 mentioned in its appendix D that SMTP could use the X.25 virtual circuit (ISO level 3) directly, but suggested running a reliable end-to-end protocol such as TCP on top. That was reasonable given how reliable the packet networks (PSDNs) were in 1981. By 1989 the author considers the service reliable enough for direct use.

The procedures are said to have proven successful in extensive production use involving 24 PSDNs in 22 different countries, and also over private X.25 connections and X.25 LANs. A virtual circuit (VC) is opened for each SMTP session, the full duplex channel carries the session, and the VC is closed, normally by the calling side.
sections.eli5: Instead of adding an extra helper on top of X.25, the mail just uses X.25's own connection, one call per mail session.

sections.title: Calls, Packets and Closing
sections.content:
The first four octets of the Call User Data field, commonly a protocol identifier, should be hex C0F70000 (decimal 192 247 0 0). Implementations should let this be configured per address. Any negotiable call facilities may be used, and should be specifiable for each called address.

SMTP data may be split into packets however the sender likes, and sequences with the M bit set, up to 2048 bytes in total, are encouraged. Commands and responses are best sent as single packets, though that is not required. Q-bit packets and interrupt packets are not used and should be ignored. On a level 3 circuit reset, the VC should be cleared and the connection retried, possibly after a delay or with different facilities.

X.25 discards packets in transit when a VC is cleared, so the calling side closes the SMTP session only after it receives the Service Closing message, whether in reply to QUIT or because the service must shut down.
sections.eli5: Every call starts with a special ID code so the other side knows it is mail. When finished, the caller hangs up only after hearing the goodbye, so nothing gets lost.

sections.title: Character Code
sections.content: The character code is the full ASCII-8 code, with no escapes or modifications. Lines end with CRLF (13 10 decimal), and implementations should, if possible, also recognize lines ending only with LF (10 decimal).
sections.eli5: Letters are sent as plain ASCII, and each line ends with the usual line-break signal.

sections.title: Timeouts
sections.content:
SMTP does not normally time out a session, but on X.25 these values have proven effective. If a call accept is not received within 100 seconds, or the Service Ready message does not arrive within another 120 seconds, the call is cleared and retried later. Once established, the circuit is cleared after 10 minutes with no response. After QUIT, the timeout is shortened to 20 seconds, which can cause an ungraceful exit but does not affect completed SMTP transactions.

Permanent virtual circuits and D bit selection are not used.
sections.eli5: If the other side stays silent too long, hang up and try later. After saying goodbye, wait only a short time.

references.text: Postel, J., "Simple Mail Transfer Protocol", RFC 821, USC Information Sciences Institute, August 1982.
